Firstly, emotions aren't wrong or right. Emotions exist to tell you something about your life/body/soul. With that being said, some emotions are 'better' than others in that some don't feel great (such as your anger/jealousy). What is that anger telling you? What is that anger saying about your life at its current state?

You've got to begin with getting to the root of the feeling. You've got to ask yourself Noble Questions. Questions that demand truthful, authentic answers... the trick is, answering truthfully for yourself, and no one else. Here's a little tid bit I found regarding the topic of Noble Questions (the last bit being the most important):

We have learned to ask negative questions. I believe we learned to do this to ward off oppression by our parents and teachers as if to say: if I beat myself up, you will see it and not beat me up. Watch any little league or high school sport and you’ll see at least one kid fail and shake his head in disgust, reproach himself harshly, or scream “oh you stupid”. The kids abuse themselves so their parents won’t; it’s so sad and unnecessary.

So by asking as question, “why am I so ____”, the Universe responds with evidence that you are so ____ (fill in the blank) and becomes self-fulfilling. Not the way to create a beautiful and easy life.

I believe that we as humans define every single situation/event/occurrence that we experience as good or bad. In the true reality of it all, these experiences are exactly that... just an experience. So, it's a matter of perception. It comes back to Noble Questions.

If you keep asking yourself "why am I so sad?" that implies that you are sad. Look at these examples for more insight into what I'm trying to explain:

“How can I be even more happy?” assumes you are currently happy.

“How can I be even more healthy?” assumes you are currently healthy.

“Why am I always on time?” assumes you are always on time.

“Why do I always succeed?” assumes you always succeed.

Do you notice how your brain organizes itself differently? It starts to look for evidence of how you always succeed. If it comes up against a negative response, ask the question again: “why do I always succeed?” Notice in your body where you feel expansion, softening, relaxing or happiness.

This takes tons of practice. I've been working at self fulfillment and finding my own true happiness for years now (consciously) and I've come to realize a lot along the way. One of the biggest things is knowing when to ask the right questions to yourself and learning to answer them authentically. If you make up an answer, you'll get nothing from it. If you say what you think you're supposed to say, you'll only hurt yourself by denying the truth. Hopefully, by asking yourself these questions, you can begin to change your perception (or definition) of the breakup and the current events that clearly bring up something inside of you. Just remember, that feeling is telling you something, and nobody but yourself can decipher it. Good luck and wishing you happiness, friend!
